subject: Cognitive Science
title: Working Memory and Sentences
description: Learn Working Memory and Sentences in one minute.

hook.text: 'The rat the cat the dog chased bit escaped.' Legal grammar—but almost impossible to understand. Why?

buildup.text: Center-embedded sentences stack clauses inside each other, overwhelming working memory capacity.

discovery.text: Working memory can hold roughly 3–4 items. Each embedded clause adds another item that must be tracked.

twist.text: German and Dutch allow more embedding than English—their speakers may have slightly different processing strategies.

climax.text: Sentence complexity isn't about length—it's about how many open dependencies working memory must juggle.

punchline.text: Long sentences are fine. Stacked ones break the brain.

quiz.question: Why are center-embedded sentences so hard?

details.summary: Understanding long or complex sentences taxes working memory. Nested clauses like the cat the dog the rat bit chased ran force you to hold multiple incomplete structures simultaneously.
details.whyItMatters: Working memory constraints on sentence processing bridge linguistics and cognitive psychology. They explain why simple writing is clearer and why legal language is so hard to parse.
takeaways: Complex sentences require holding multiple structures in memory
Center-embedded clauses overload working memory capacity
Grammar generates structures that cognition cannot process

faq.question: Why are center-embedded sentences so hard?
faq.answer: Each nested clause pushes an incomplete structure onto working memory's stack. By the third embedding, you must track three subjects and three verbs simultaneously. This exceeds working memory capacity for most people.

faq.question: How does this affect writing and communication?
faq.answer: Clear communication respects working memory limits. Short sentences with one main clause are easiest to process. Legal documents, academic prose, and bureaucratic language often fail because they pile complexity that exceeds readers' processing capacity.
